nameStory: The 'hairy groundcherry' gets its name from two obvious features: the dense, fuzzy hairs covering its stems and leaves, and the way its fruits eventually drop to the ground still wrapped in their papery husks. The 'cherry' part is a bit misleading since it's not related to true cherries at all, but the small, round fruits do resemble tiny cherries when you peek inside their lantern-like cases.
description: Hairy groundcherry is a low-growing annual herb that rarely gets taller than your knee, maxing out around 2 feet tall. This fuzzy little plant belongs to the nightshade family, making it a cousin to tomatoes and peppers. It produces small yellow bell-shaped flowers with distinctive dark spots in their throats, followed by marble-sized fruits wrapped in inflated, papery husks that look like tiny Chinese lanterns. The whole plant has a soft, velvety texture from its dense covering of fine hairs.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: The distinctive inflated, papery husk surrounding each fruit looks like a miniature ribbed lantern, feeling crisp and dry when mature, containing a small berry inside

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow bell-shaped flowers about half an inch long with five dark purple or brown spots inside the throat and blue-tipped stamens

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual herb with densely hairy, glandular stems that feel soft and slightly sticky to the touch, rarely exceeding 2 feet tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to heart-shaped leaves 1-3 inches long with smooth or slightly toothed edges, covered in soft, dense hairs that give them a velvety texture

habitat: In New England, hairy groundcherry is quite rare and typically found in disturbed soils like gardens, farm edges, and waste areas where the ground has been recently worked. It prefers sunny spots with well-drained soil and can tolerate poor or sandy conditions. Look for it in areas with some human disturbance rather than pristine natural habitats.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge with their characteristic fuzzy leaves, beginning to establish their low, spreading growth pattern.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower throughout the summer months, producing their distinctive yellow blooms with dark throat spots. Early fruits begin forming inside their developing papery husks.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen and the papery husks turn tan and crispy, eventually dropping to the ground. The entire plant dies back with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Only dried husks and seeds remain, with the annual plants completely gone until spring germination.

funFact: Despite being called a 'cherry,' this plant is actually more closely related to your breakfast tomato than to any cherry tree - and those distinctive dark spots in the flower's throat act like landing strips to guide bees straight to the nectar!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, you're more likely to encounter its cousin the clammy groundcherry, which has similar papery husks but smoother, less hairy stems and leaves - run your fingers along the stem and you'll feel the difference immediately.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'groundcherry' can be confusing since these aren't cherries at all, but members of the nightshade family. Some people also call them 'husk tomatoes,' which actually makes more sense given their relationship to tomatoes and their papery-wrapped fruits.
compareHints: Among New England's groundcherries, hairy groundcherry stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, glandular stems and leaves that feel almost velvety. Clammy groundcherry has sticky but smoother foliage, while long-leaved groundcherry has much narrower leaves and less dense hair covering. The intensity of the fuzziness is your best clue - if it feels like soft velvet, you've likely found the hairy species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's groundcherries, clammy groundcherry stands out for its distinctly sticky texture – other species like hairy groundcherry are fuzzy but not sticky, while strawberry groundcherry tends to be more smooth.
